name: Shoulder Impingement (Subacromial Pain Syndrome)
secondary_queries: shoulder pain when lifting arm overhead
seo_title: Shoulder Impingement Treatment | First Rehab N. Palm Beach
seo_desc: Shoulder pain when you reach overhead? Impingement, bursitis and tendinitis care in North Palm Beach with one-on-one PT since 1991. Call 561-624-4263.
lede: Shoulder impingement makes reaching overhead painful, and a guided exercise program is the first-choice treatment for calming the irritated tendons and bursa.
what_it_is: The top of your shoulder blade forms a bony roof called the acromion. Under it, the rotator cuff tendons and a small fluid-filled sac called the bursa glide each time you raise your arm. When the tendons are irritated (tendinitis), the bursa is inflamed (bursitis), or the space gets crowded, lifting the arm can pinch these tissues against the acromion. Clinicians increasingly call this group of problems subacromial pain syndrome.

According to Cleveland Clinic, impingement is estimated to cause around half of all shoulder pain. It is common in swimmers, baseball, tennis and volleyball players, and in jobs with repeated overhead work such as construction and painting. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons notes that rotator cuff pain is common in both young athletes and older people.
symptoms: Pain at the front or outside of the shoulder that may spread down the upper arm
Pain when raising your arm overhead or reaching out
Mild pain at rest as well as with activity
Pain at night, especially lying on the affected side
Tenderness or swelling at the front of the shoulder
Trouble getting dressed, fastening a seatbelt, or brushing your hair
causes: Repetitive overhead motion in sports or work
Overhead sports such as swimming, baseball, tennis and volleyball
Jobs such as construction, painting and window washing
Irritated rotator cuff tendons or an inflamed bursa
Less commonly, a fall or other sudden trauma

how_therapy_helps.intro: Exercise is the main treatment. The 2025 rotator cuff tendinopathy clinical practice guideline in JOSPT recommends an active rehabilitation program, which may include motor control and resistance training, as an initial treatment to reduce pain and disability. It supports manual therapy, alone or with exercise, for short-term pain relief, and it notes that corticosteroid injections, which physicians give, may reduce pain and short-term disability. Cleveland Clinic notes that people usually start feeling better a few weeks after starting treatment.
methods: Rotator cuff and shoulder blade exercises start at a load your shoulder tolerates and build over weeks, the approach the JOSPT guideline recommends as an initial treatment.
You practice raising and lowering the arm with better shoulder blade movement and timing, so the tendons are loaded more evenly.
Hands-on work to the shoulder, upper back or neck may ease pain in the short term and make exercise easier to tolerate.
Self-stretches restore normal shoulder motion where tightness is limiting comfortable reaching.
Your therapist helps adjust overhead tasks, training volume and posture, and the guideline supports ergonomic changes for work-related shoulder pain.

first_visit: Your evaluation compares motion in both shoulders, notes where in the lifting arc pain begins, and tests rotator cuff strength in several positions. Your therapist watches how your shoulder blade moves, checks posture and neck motion, and asks about the sport or job tasks that bring on symptoms. Those findings set the starting load for your exercises, which begin at that first visit.
recovery: Expect gradual change over weeks and months. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons says complete recovery with nonsurgical treatment can take several weeks to months. Cleveland Clinic notes that people usually start feeling better a few weeks after starting treatment, that complete healing typically takes several months, and that some people need treatment and rehab for up to a year. Long-standing symptoms, heavy overhead demands and returning to full training too fast can all slow things down.
self_care: Take a break from the overhead activity that triggers your pain, instead of resting the whole arm.
Ice the front and side of the shoulder to calm soreness.
Avoid slumping with your head forward and shoulders rounded, especially at a desk.
Keep using the arm for everyday tasks that do not provoke pain.
see_a_doctor: Call 911 if shoulder pain comes with shortness of breath, a tight chest or sweating, since these can be signs of a heart attack.
A shoulder that looks deformed after a fall needs urgent care or an emergency room.
Being unable to move your arm away from your body after an injury needs urgent evaluation.
Intense pain or sudden swelling after an accident needs urgent care.
Redness, warmth and tenderness around the joint, or pain that keeps getting worse, should be checked by a physician.

faqs.q: What is the difference between shoulder impingement, bursitis and rotator cuff tendinitis?
faqs.a: They are closely related and often occur together. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons explains that tendinitis is irritation of the rotator cuff tendons, bursitis is inflammation of the bursa above them, and impingement describes the acromion rubbing on those tissues as you lift your arm. Subacromial pain syndrome is a newer umbrella term for this whole group of problems.

faqs.q: Can shoulder impingement heal on its own?
faqs.a: Some mild cases calm down with rest from the aggravating activity, which the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons lists as a first step along with anti-inflammatory medication. Pain that keeps returning, wakes you at night or limits daily tasks usually needs a structured exercise program. Continuing to push through painful overhead work tends to keep the tissues irritated.

The 2025 JOSPT rotator cuff tendinopathy guideline recommends an active program built on motor control and resistance training, using loads that are progressed over time. That usually means rotator cuff and shoulder blade strengthening, practice moving the arm with good shoulder blade control, and stretches for tight areas. Starting loads matter, so a therapist typically sets them after an evaluation.

faqs.q: Should I stop working out with shoulder impingement?
faqs.a: You usually do not need to stop exercising altogether. The aim is to cut back on the movements that clearly provoke pain, often heavy pressing or repeated overhead work, while keeping the rest of your training going. APTA's ChoosePT guide describes a gradual return to demanding activities with proper mechanics once strength and motion improve.

faqs.q: Is a cortisone shot better than physical therapy for shoulder impingement?
faqs.a: The 2025 JOSPT guideline says corticosteroid injections may reduce pain and short-term disability, and it recommends an active exercise program as the initial treatment. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons describes an injection as an option when rest, medication and therapy have not brought relief. Injections are given by physicians.

faqs.q: When is surgery needed for shoulder impingement?
faqs.a: The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons recommends considering surgery when nonsurgical treatment does not relieve pain. The usual procedure is arthroscopic, removing the inflamed bursa and part of the acromion to create more space. OrthoInfo notes that it can take 2 to 4 months after surgery to achieve complete pain relief, and in some cases up to a year.

notes_for_reviewer: ICD-10 M75.4 (Impingement syndrome of shoulder) verified on icd10data.com as a category; laterality subcodes apply. Related: M75.5 bursitis of shoulder, M75.3 calcific tendinitis.
The JOSPT 2025 guideline is for rotator cuff tendinopathy; applying it to subacromial pain syndrome reflects common usage but please confirm you are comfortable with that framing.
The 'half of all shoulder pain' estimate is Cleveland Clinic's wording ('experts estimate'); confirm you want it published.
The guideline also mentions taping, acupuncture, shockwave and laser (calcific cases); these were omitted as they are outside the clinic's listed services.
The self-care tip on icing is drawn from Cleveland Clinic's treatment list (icing); exact durations were not given in the source, so none are stated.

Fact-check: the 2025 JOSPT CPG statement 'should not be used as a first-line treatment' applies to hyaluronic acid injections, not corticosteroid injections; the corticosteroid recommendation is that clinicians 'may' use them to reduce pain and short-term disability. The 'advises against therapeutic ultrasound' claim was only confirmed for calcific tendinopathy and was removed. Grade/strength of the active-rehab recommendation was not confirmed, so 'strongest' was removed.
